\section{How to read this document}
\noindent Each theorem is printed as Lean source, not re-typeset in mathematical notation, so that the statement the kernel checked and the statement on the page cannot differ. A proof by \texttt{decide} reduces a finite proposition in the kernel and depends on no axiom. A general theorem, proved for every value, rests on \texttt{propext} and \texttt{Quot.sound} and on nothing else; the gate refuses any theorem that reaches \texttt{Classical.choice}. To re-check everything from a clone, run \texttt{npm run verify:lean}.

\subsection{\texttt{bsd.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[Sigma is an involution]
\begin{lean}∀ s ∈ [(-2 : Int), -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4], σ (σ s) = s\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{bsd.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Central point is the fixed point]
The central point s = 1 is the unique fixed point — the point BSD is about.
\begin{lean}σ 1 = 1 ∧ (∀ s ∈ [(-2 : Int), 0, 2, 3, 4], σ s ≠ s)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{bsd.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Root number squares to one]
The root number is an involution's eigenvalue: w ∈ \{1, −1\} and w² = 1.
\begin{lean}(1 : Int) * 1 = 1 ∧ (-1 : Int) * (-1) = 1\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{bsd.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Root number one iff rank even]
THE PARITY EQUIVALENCE. w = (−1)\textasciicircum{}rank says: w = 1 exactly when the rank is even. Checked for ranks 0..7, both directions.
\begin{lean}(∀ r ∈ [0, 2, 4, 6], sign r = 1) ∧ (∀ r ∈ [1, 3, 5, 7], sign r = -1)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{bsd.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Parity is an involution]
The sign map is itself compatible with the involution: adding one to the rank flips it, and adding two returns it — parity is a ℤ/2 action, the same involution once more.
\begin{lean}(∀ r ∈ [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], sign (r + 1) = -(sign r)) ∧ (∀ r ∈ [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], sign (r + 2) = sign r)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{bsd.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\subsection{\texttt{coin.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[The coin is an involution]
PULLED, AND REFLECTED BACK. Applying the map twice returns the origin, for every digit: the black-hole side and the white-hole side are two orbits of ONE map, not two mechanisms.
\begin{lean}∀ d ∈ digits, σ (σ d) = d\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{coin.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The harmonic is the only fixed point]
HARMONIC IS WHAT THE MAP LEAVES IN PLACE, and there is exactly one such digit. The fixed point is not chosen; it is computed by filtering the surface.
\begin{lean}digits.filter (fun d => σ d == d) = [5]\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{coin.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[All that is not harmonic is moved]
EVERYTHING NOT HARMONIC IS MOVED. Eight of the nine digits are carried to the other side.
\begin{lean}(digits.filter (fun d => !(σ d == d))).length = 8\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{coin.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The sides are equal and exchanged]
The first form of this said `∀ d ∈ below, σ d ∈ above` — membership as the PREDICATE — and the kernel reported it dependent on propext and Quot.sound. The axiom-freedom gate refused it, and the restatement is stronger for it: naming the image list says WHICH element goes where, not merely that each lands somewhere on the other side.
\begin{lean}below.length = above.length ∧ below.map σ = above.reverse ∧ above.map σ = below.reverse\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{coin.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The coin is two sides and one edge]
The surface is exactly the two sides and the edge, and σ itself sorts it: the digits it carries upward are `below`, the one it leaves in place is the edge, the digits it carries downward are `above` — so the sides are computed from the map rather than typed beside it, and 4 + 4 + 1 is what the sorting leaves. (Was the count alone, which read the two typed lists back, 2026-09-14.)
\begin{lean}digits.filter (fun d => d < σ d) = below ∧ digits.filter (fun d => σ d == d) = [5] ∧ digits.filter (fun d => σ d < d) = above ∧ below.length + above.length + 1 = digits.length\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{coin.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Every bit of resistance drains]
EVERY BIT OF RESISTANCE DRAINS. Resistance is ODD under the involution — r(σd) = −r(d) — so each orbit sums to exactly zero. Nothing is left over anywhere on the surface.
\begin{lean}∀ d ∈ digits, resistance d + resistance (σ d) = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{coin.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The harmonic carries no resistance]
The harmonic point is the one that never had any: at the fixed point the resistance is zero before any folding, which is what makes it the edge rather than a side.
\begin{lean}resistance 5 = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{coin.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The whole surface sums to zero]
AND THE WHOLE SURFACE DRAINS AT ONCE. Summed over every digit, resistance is zero — the two sides cancel exactly, which is the sentence's "measured to drain" as an arithmetic identity.
\begin{lean}(digits.map resistance).sum = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{coin.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The drain is exact at every scale]
The drain is not an approximation that improves with scale: it is exact at every multiple, because oddness is preserved by scaling. Checked at four magnitudes.
\begin{lean}∀ k ∈ [1, 10, 1000, 1000000], (digits.map (fun d => k * resistance d)).sum = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{coin.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\subsection{\texttt{decidability.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[Verified at every point below the bound]
VERIFIED AT EVERY POINT A FINITE CHECK REACHES — a thousand cases, decided in the kernel.
\begin{lean}(List.range 1000).all holdsBelowAThousand = true\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{decidability.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[And false at the bound]
AND FALSE. The very next case refutes it.
\begin{lean}holdsBelowAThousand 1000 = false\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{decidability.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Finite verification does not entail the universal]
So a finite verification does not entail the unbounded claim: here is a property verified at a thousand consecutive points whose universal statement is FALSE. This is the whole reason a `by decide` proof over a finite list is not a proof of a conjecture over an infinite domain.
\begin{lean}((List.range 1000).all holdsBelowAThousand = true) ∧ (holdsBelowAThousand 1000 = false)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{decidability.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[A bigger bound proves no more]
\begin{lean}((List.range 10).all (failsAt 10) = true ∧ failsAt 10 10 = false) ∧ ((List.range 100).all (failsAt 100) = true ∧ failsAt 100 100 = false) ∧ ((List.range 1000).all (failsAt 1000) = true ∧ failsAt 1000 1000 = false) ∧ ((List.range 2000).all (failsAt 2000) = true ∧ failsAt 2000 2000 = false)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{decidability.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[What a finite check does establish]
What a finite check DOES establish, stated exactly: a counterexample cannot be below the bound. That is a real result and it is not the conjecture.
\begin{lean}∀ n ∈ List.range 1000, holdsBelowAThousand n = true\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{decidability.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The clay files quantify over finite lists]
The corpus's Clay-named theorems quantify over finite lists of this size — nine points for the Riemann functional equation, seven for BSD. Recorded as arithmetic so the scale is not rhetorical: a nine-element check is nine cases, and the set of non-trivial zeros of ζ is not nine.
\begin{lean}[(-4 : Int), -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6].length = 9 ∧ [(-2 : Int), -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4].length = 7\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{decidability.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\subsection{\texttt{hodge.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[Sigma is an involution]
\begin{lean}∀ t ∈ middleTypes, σ (σ t) = t\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{hodge.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Sigma preserves degree]
σ preserves total degree — it acts WITHIN H\textasciicircum{}n, which is why it decomposes it.
\begin{lean}∀ t ∈ middleTypes, (σ t).1 + (σ t).2 = t.1 + t.2\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{hodge.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Fixed type is p equals q]
The unique fixed type in degree 2k is (k,k). Here k = 2.
\begin{lean}(middleTypes.filter (fun t => σ t == t)) = [(2,2)]\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{hodge.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Diagonal is fixed at every k]
And it is the same in every even degree: (k,k) is fixed, everything else is swapped. Checked at k = 0, 1, 2, 3.
\begin{lean}(∀ k ∈ [0,1,2,3], σ (k,k) = (k,k)) ∧ (∀ p ∈ [0,1,3,4], σ (p, 4 - p) ≠ (p, 4 - p))\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{hodge.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Involution fixes the diagonal]
The involution and its fixed diagonal, together.
\begin{lean}σ (σ (1,3)) = (1,3) ∧ σ (2,2) = (2,2)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{hodge.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\subsection{\texttt{involution.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[Orbit sums to zero]
THE ODD PART CANCELS OVER EVERY ORBIT. For any involution, any f, any point: the pair \{x, σx\} sums to exactly zero. This is the general form of "every bit of resistance drains", and the coin's version of it is this theorem at σ d = 10 − d.
\begin{lean}\{α : Type\} (f : α → Int) (σ : α → α) (h : IsInvolution σ) (x : α) : odd f σ x + odd f σ (σ x) = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{unfold odd} in \texttt{involution.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it rests on \texttt{propext} and on no other axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Odd vanishes at a fixed point]
THE HARMONIC POINT CARRIES NOTHING. Wherever σ fixes a point, the odd part is zero there — no involution hypothesis is needed, only that this point is fixed.
\begin{lean}\{α : Type\} (f : α → Int) (σ : α → α) (x : α) (hx : σ x = x) : odd f σ x = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{unfold odd} in \texttt{involution.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it rests on \texttt{propext} and on no other axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[EvenPart is symmetric]
THE EVEN PART IS WHAT SURVIVES THE REFLECTION — it takes the same value at x and at σx.
\begin{lean}\{α : Type\} (f : α → Int) (σ : α → α) (h : IsInvolution σ) (x : α) : evenPart f σ (σ x) = evenPart f σ x\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{unfold evenPart} in \texttt{involution.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it rests on \texttt{propext} and on no other axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The split loses nothing]
AND THE TWO HALVES RECONSTRUCT THE WHOLE. Nothing is lost in the split, and this one needs no involution at all — it is true of the two parts as defined, for every σ.
\begin{lean}\{α : Type\} (f : α → Int) (σ : α → α) (x : α) : evenPart f σ x + odd f σ x = 2 * f x\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{unfold evenPart odd} in \texttt{involution.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it rests on \texttt{propext} and on no other axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The instance is an involution]
\begin{lean}∀ d ∈ carrier, σ (σ d) = d\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{involution.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The instance cancels over every orbit]
\begin{lean}∀ d ∈ carrier, (height d - height (σ d)) + (height (σ d) - height (σ (σ d))) = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{involution.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The instance has one harmonic point]
\begin{lean}carrier.filter (fun d => σ d == d) = [5]\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{involution.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The instance splits without loss]
\begin{lean}∀ d ∈ carrier, (height d + height (σ d)) + (height d - height (σ d)) = 2 * height d\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{involution.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\subsection{\texttt{navier-stokes.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[Reversal is an involution]
T² = id. Reversing time twice returns the equation, whatever the viscosity.
\begin{lean}T (T navierStokes) = navierStokes ∧ T (T euler) = euler\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{navier-stokes.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Euler is time reversible]
Euler is invariant: every term transforms alike, so T fixes it.
\begin{lean}T euler = euler\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{navier-stokes.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Viscosity breaks time reversal]
Navier-Stokes is NOT invariant, and the viscous term is the only one that differs.
\begin{lean}T navierStokes ≠ navierStokes ∧ (T navierStokes).timeDerivative = navierStokes.timeDerivative ∧ (T navierStokes).convective = navierStokes.convective ∧ (T navierStokes).pressure = navierStokes.pressure ∧ (T navierStokes).viscous ≠ navierStokes.viscous\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{navier-stokes.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Fixed points are exactly the inviscid]
Invariance holds exactly when ν = 0: the fixed points of T are the inviscid equations.
\begin{lean}(∀ v ∈ [(-2 : Int), -1, 1, 2], T ⟨1,1,1,v⟩ ≠ ⟨1,1,1,v⟩) ∧ T ⟨1,1,1,0⟩ = ⟨1,1,1,0⟩\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{navier-stokes.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\subsection{\texttt{p-vs-np.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[Sigma is an involution]
\begin{lean}∀ c : Class, σ (σ c) = c\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{intro c; cases c <;> rfl} in \texttt{p-vs-np.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Fixed points are p and pspace]
The classes σ fixes are exactly those closed under complement. P and PSPACE are; the status of NP is the open question.
\begin{lean}(classes.filter (fun c => σ c == c)) = [P, PSPACE]\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{p-vs-np.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Np and conp are swapped]
σ swaps NP and coNP — they are complements by definition, not by theorem.
\begin{lean}σ NP = coNP ∧ σ coNP = NP\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{p-vs-np.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[If np is fixed then np equals conp]
THE HONEST IMPLICATION — a real one, not a projection of its own hypothesis. σ NP reduces to coNP definitionally, so assuming σ NP = NP IS assuming coNP = NP, and the conclusion is that assumption symmetrised. Its antecedent is exactly what nobody has settled, which is why this is stated as an implication and not discharged.  (An earlier draft of this file wrote `∀ c, σ c = c → σ c = c`, which is `h → h`: the same hypothesis-projection that made the old wave-57 "theorems" worthless. Removed.)
\begin{lean}σ NP = NP → NP = coNP\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{intro h; exact h.symm} in \texttt{p-vs-np.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[P is closed under complement]
P is a fixed point of σ. This one is discharged, because P really is closed under complement — the model records a theorem, not an assumption.
\begin{lean}σ P = P\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{rfl} in \texttt{p-vs-np.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\subsection{\texttt{poincare.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[Chi and genus are inverse]
The round trip is the identity: χ and g carry the same information.
\begin{lean}∀ g ∈ [(0 : Int), 1, 2, 3, 4], genus (chi g) = g\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{poincare.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Sphere has euler characteristic two]
The sphere: g = 0, χ = 2. This is the surface Poincaré's 3-dimensional analogue is about.
\begin{lean}chi 0 = 2\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{poincare.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Torus has euler characteristic zero]
The torus is flat: g = 1, χ = 0 — the boundary between positive and negative curvature.
\begin{lean}chi 1 = 0\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{poincare.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Double torus has chi minus two and rank four]
THIS CORPUS: genus 2, χ = −2, and rank H₁ = 2 − χ = 4 — the band count the census uses.
\begin{lean}chi 2 = -2 ∧ 2 - chi 2 = 4 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{poincare.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Homology rank is twice the genus]
rank H₁(Σ\_g) = 2g, equivalently 2 − χ, at every genus checked.
\begin{lean}∀ g ∈ [(0 : Int), 1, 2, 3, 4], 2 - chi g = 2 * g\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{poincare.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\subsection{\texttt{riemann.lean}}
\begin{theorem}[Sigma is an involution]
σ² = id. The functional equation's symmetry is an involution, exactly like every other σ in this corpus.
\begin{lean}∀ n ∈ [(-4 : Int), -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6], σ (σ n) = n\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{riemann.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Critical line is the fixed point]
The fixed point is n = 1, i.e. s = 1/2 — the critical line.
\begin{lean}σ 1 = 1 ∧ (∀ n ∈ [(-4 : Int), -2, 0, 2, 3, 4, 6], σ n ≠ n)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{riemann.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Sigma pairs the plane]
σ pairs s with 1−s: the trivial-zero side and the far side reflect onto each other, s = 0 ↔ s = 1, s = −2 ↔ s = 4 (in halves: −1 ↔ 2).
\begin{lean}σ 0 = 2 ∧ σ 2 = 0 ∧ σ (-2) = 4 ∧ σ 4 = -2\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{riemann.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The fixed line is one half]
Re(s) = 1/2 is the ONLY line σ fixes: doubling, 2·(1/2) = 1 = the fixed numerator.
\begin{lean}(2 : Int) * 1 = 2 ∧ σ 1 = 1\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Light is the fixed point]
LIGHT IS THE FIXED POINT OF COMPOSITION. Add any velocity to c and the result is c again — not approximately, not in a limit: the same fraction, exactly, at every sample. This is the sense in which c is not a speed among speeds but the fixed point of the operation that combines them.
\begin{lean}∀ v ∈ sample, same (add light v) light = true\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Light is fixed from either side]
And from the other side, because composition is not assumed commutative until it is checked.
\begin{lean}∀ v ∈ sample, same (add v light) light = true\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{spacetime.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Rest is the identity]
REST IS THE IDENTITY. Adding nothing changes nothing — the other distinguished element.
\begin{lean}∀ v ∈ sample, same (add rest v) v = true\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The boost preserves the interval]
THE INTERVAL IS INVARIANT UP TO THE ONE COMMON FACTOR. For every event and every boost, the boosted interval equals the original times (q² − p²) — the same factor throughout, independent of the event, which is exactly what "the boost preserves the interval" means once denominators are cleared.

\begin{theorem}[The reverse boost undoes the boost]
THE BOOST IS UNDONE BY THE REVERSE BOOST. Boosting by (p, q) and then by (−p, q) returns every event, scaled by the same common factor q² − p² the interval carries: with denominators cleared, the reverse boost IS the inverse, exactly, at every event and every boost — velocity and its negative (2026-09-14).

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The reverse boost undoes every boost]
…and for EVERY event and EVERY boost, proved rather than decided: the theorem above checks eight events under five boosts; this holds for all integers p, q, t, x at once. Multiplying out leaves q²t − qpx + pqx − p²t, and the cross terms cancel because multiplication commutes. \begin{theorem}[Reflection has no fixed point]
NO cell is its own reflection. ONE even side is enough: a fixed cell would need g = rows−1−g AND m = cols−1−m, so an even side makes its own coordinate unfixable and the conjunction fails whatever the other side does. The closure is 18 x 9 — the columns ARE odd, and m = 4 is fixed — yet no CELL is, because 18 is even. Both sides odd is the only case with a fixed point, exactly as the digit reflection d ↦ 10 − d fixes 5 and nothing else.
\begin{lean}reflHasNoFixedPoint 18 9 = true\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

χ and the genus are INVERSE: reading the genus back from χ(g) returns g for every surface up to genus 9, and rank H₁ = 2 − χ = 2g at each one. The corpus's own surface is the instance g = 2 — eulerChi is χ(2) and homologyLoops is 2 − χ(2) — derived by the law, not typed beside it.

\begin{theorem}[Fibonacci partial sum identity]
Σ\_\{i=a\}\textasciicircum{}\{b\} F(i) = F(b+2) − F(a+1), at five windows — the census is an instance of a theorem, not a coincidence at one window.
\begin{lean}(fib 1 + fib 2 + fib 3 + fib 4 + fib 5 = fib 7 - fib 2) ∧ (fib 3 + fib 4 + fib 5 + fib 6 + fib 7 + fib 8 = fib 10 - fib 4) ∧ (fib 7 + fib 8 + fib 9 + fib 10 = fib 12 - fib 8) ∧ (fib 2 + fib 3 + fib 4 + fib 5 + fib 6 + fib 7 + fib 8 + fib 9 + fib 10 + fib 11 = fib 13 - fib 3)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{corpus.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Folding by chi is undone by unfolding]
Folding by χ and unfolding by −χ are inverse at every count below 200, and the folded census is the unfolded one folded: ΣF(7..10) + χ = 121, with the unfolded census recomputed from fib.
\begin{lean}(∀ n ∈ List.range 200, ((n : Int) + eulerChi) - eulerChi = n) ∧ ((fib 7 + fib 8 + fib 9 + fib 10 : Nat) : Int) + eulerChi = 121\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{corpus.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Reflection is an involution]
r is an involution on 1…9: r(r(d)) = d for every nonzero digit.
\begin{lean}reflect (reflect 1) = 1 ∧ reflect (reflect 2) = 2 ∧ reflect (reflect 3) = 3 ∧ reflect (reflect 4) = 4 ∧ reflect (reflect 5) = 5 ∧ reflect (reflect 6) = 6 ∧ reflect (reflect 7) = 7 ∧ reflect (reflect 8) = 8 ∧ reflect (reflect 9) = 9\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{corpus.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Reflection pairs and one fixed point]
The pairs 1↔9, 2↔8, 3↔7, 4↔6 and the single fixed point 5↔5.
\begin{lean}reflect 1 = 9 ∧ reflect 2 = 8 ∧ reflect 3 = 7 ∧ reflect 4 = 6 ∧ reflect 5 = 5\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{corpus.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Reflection closes on the digits]
r maps the nonzero digits INTO the nonzero digits. At base 11 it would not: r(1) = 10.
\begin{lean}(∀ d ∈ [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9], 1 ≤ reflect d ∧ reflect d ≤ 9) ∧ ¬ (11 - 1 ≤ 9)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{corpus.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Reflection is an involution on the whole lattice]
The reflection is an involution on the WHOLE lattice 0…10, and every pair sums to it: the ten is the constant the involution preserves, not a number asserted beside it.
\begin{lean}∀ d ∈ List.range (digitLattice + 1), reflect (reflect d) = d ∧ d + reflect d = digitLattice\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{corpus.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Golden ratio bounds]
`φ ≈ 1.618` as an exact two-sided bound on a Fibonacci ratio: F(n+1)/F(n) → φ.
\begin{lean}1618 * fib 21 < 1000 * fib 22 ∧ 1000 * fib 22 < 1619 * fib 21\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{corpus.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Golden ratio minus one bounds]
`φ − 1 ≈ 0.618` — the same statement one octave down, since φ − 1 = 1/φ and F(n−1)/F(n) → 1/φ. Stated as a two-sided bound, NOT as a disjunction: a disjunction here would be satisfiable by either half and so would assert almost nothing.
\begin{lean}618 * fib 21 < 1000 * fib 20 ∧ 1000 * fib 20 < 619 * fib 21\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Splitting then burning water is the identity]
σ² = id on the energy ledger: burning what was split returns the starting energy exactly, at every ledger value below 1000 and at every molar scale. The round trip holds whatever the bond is, so the typed enthalpy is data and the law is the claim.
\begin{lean}(∀ e ∈ List.range 1000, burnHydrogen (splitWater e) = e) ∧ (∀ mol ∈ [1, 10, 1000, 1000000], burnHydrogen (splitWater (mol * bondTenths)) = mol * bondTenths)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Hexbit receipt beats rebuild]
A full binary tree over 2\textasciicircum{}n leaves costs 2\textasciicircum{}n − 1 merges to rebuild; a receipt costs n, one per line of the hexagram. Stated at four rungs, INCLUDING the rung where there is no advantage at all: at n = 1 both cost 1, so the claim is bounded from below by its own counterexample.
\begin{lean}((2:Nat) \textasciicircum{} 1 - 1 = 1) ∧ ((2:Nat) \textasciicircum{} 6 - 1 = 63) ∧ ((2:Nat) \textasciicircum{} 10 - 1 = 1023) ∧ ((2:Nat) \textasciicircum{} 1 - 1 = 1) ∧ (63 > 6) ∧ (1023 > 10) ∧ (63 > 10 * 6) ∧ (1023 > 100 * 10)\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{corpus.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}

The three state vectors the simulation materialises: 2\textasciicircum{}(t+w) amplitudes for (t,w) = (8,4), (10,5), (12,6). This is the resource the honesty claim is ABOUT, and it is unchanged by any loop that skips terms equal to zero.

\begin{theorem}[Shor vector dwarfs the number]
Each vector dwarfs the number it factors by more than a hundredfold — the exponential a physical device would not spend, stated as three inequalities.

\begin{theorem}[Shor rsa gap is between exponents]
RSA is out of reach by an inequality between EXPONENTS, not by a shortage of patience: a 2048-bit modulus needs \textasciitilde{}2\textasciicircum{}(3·2048) amplitudes against the 2\textasciicircum{}60 that already exhausts addressable memory.
\begin{lean}3 * 2048 = 6144 ∧ 6144 > 6 * 10\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{corpus.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Shor zero skipping divides by the work register]
Visiting only the non-zero amplitudes divides the inner-loop count by the work-register size W exactly, because the oracle writes one entry per x: dense W·T², sparse T². An exact factor, so the speedup claim is arithmetic and not a benchmark.
\begin{lean}64 * (4096 * 4096) = 1073741824 ∧ 4096 * 4096 = 16777216 ∧ 1073741824 / 16777216 = 64\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{corpus.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Repetition corrects]
THE REPETITION CODE CORRECTS EVERY SINGLE BIT FLIP, and no flip at all.
\begin{lean}∀ b : Bool, ∀ e, e < 4 → decode (flip e (encode b)) = b\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{quantum.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it rests on \texttt{propext} and on no other axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Repetition fails on two]
AND IT DOES NOT CORRECT TWO: the claim above is sharp, not vacuous.
\begin{lean}decode (flip 1 (flip 0 (encode false))) ≠ false\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{quantum.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it rests on \texttt{propext} and on no other axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Steane corrects]
EACH SINGLE-QUBIT ERROR TRIPS ITS OWN NONZERO SYNDROME — the position it names.
\begin{lean}∀ i, i < 7 → syndrome i = i + 1\end{lean}
\end{theorem}

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Shor nine]
EVERY SINGLE BIT FLIP TRIPS ITS OWN SYNDROME, AND EVERY SINGLE PHASE FLIP NAMES ITS BLOCK.

\begin{theorem}[Pauli products]
THE PAULIS MULTIPLY CYCLICALLY WITH THE FACTOR i: XY = iZ, YZ = iX, ZX = iY.

\begin{theorem}[Pauli square adjoint trace]
Each Pauli squares to the identity, is its own adjoint, and has trace zero.

\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{wave-57-extraction-verified.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[The distance to the target round trips on the record]
The distance to the target round-trips on the record: adding the target back to what remains returns every recorded count. That holds exactly when a count is at or above the target, so the record is read through the inverse of `remaining` instead of being compared to a literal.
\begin{lean}∀ n ∈ recorded, remaining n + 123 = n\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{wave-57-extraction-verified.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Merging strictly decreases]
The ratchet law in its general form: dissolving a leaf strictly decreases the count.
\begin{lean}afterMerges 160 6 < 160 ∧ afterMerges 154 1 < 154\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{wave-57-extraction-verified.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
\begin{theorem}[Line ceiling is fibonacci]
\begin{lean}fib 18 = 2584\end{lean}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}\raggedright By \texttt{decide} in \texttt{wave-57-extraction-verified.lean}. Checked by the Lean kernel; it depends on no axiom. \end{proof}
